title: Why does ice float?
subtitle: Water & molecules
subject: sciences
description: Ice floats on water. This seems normal, but it is actually very rare. And fortunately for life on Earth.

hero.hook: If the ice flowed, the lakes would freeze to the bottom. And life in the water would have difficulty surviving.

blocks.text: An ice cube in a glass, an iceberg in the ocean: the ice **floats**. We find it banal. However, for most substances, the solid is more **dense**, therefore heavier for the same volume: it sinks.
Water does the opposite. This exception comes from the shape of its molecule. And it saved many lakes in winter.

A water molecule is an atom of **oxygen** connected to two atoms of **hydrogen**. It is not straight: it forms a **V**. Because of this shape, the electric charges are not distributed equally: the molecule is **polar**, with one end slightly negative and the other slightly positive.

blocks.caption: The water molecule: a V that attracts and repels its neighbors.

blocks.text: Result: water molecules attract each other by [[Hydrogen bonds]], like small magnets. In the liquid, they remain close but still move. In ice, they freeze differently.

sections.title: When water freezes, it takes up space

blocks.text: Around **0 °C**, the water solidifies. To form ice, the molecules organize themselves into a **hexagonal** network, a sort of six-sided honeycomb. They then leave more **empty** between them than in the liquid state.
This is why a full bottle of water can **burst** in the freezer: ice takes up more volume than liquid water.

Less material in the same volume means: **less dense**. However, an object less dense than the liquid around it rises. Ice therefore floats on water. This is called the **water expansion abnormality**: unlike almost all substances, water expands as it cools under **4 °C**.

blocks.caption: An iceberg floats because ice is less dense than liquid water.

blocks.text: Imagine if the ice cream flowed. It would form on the surface, then sink to the bottom. The lake would freeze layer by layer, all the way to the bottom. Summer often wouldn't be enough to melt everything away.

Fortunately, the ice remains at the top. It forms a **insulating cover**. Below the frozen surface, liquid water can remain around **4 °C**, the temperature where liquid water is densest, enough for fish and aquatic plants to survive.

The white ice floe reflects a large part of the Sun's light back into space thanks to its high **albedo**, its reflective power. If it disappears, the dark ocean absorbs more heat. This accelerates warming: a vicious circle.
Ice floats because, as it solidifies, water forms a more “aerated” network: it becomes less dense than liquid water. This exception protects aquatic life in winter.
